claim: Data from 485 healthy individuals (age: 29.1 ± 3.5 years, 202 females) were obtained from the 500-subject release of the Human Connectome Project (HCP RRID:SCR_008749) database from March 2015.
source: Data from 485 healthy individuals (age: 29.1 ± 3.5 years, 202 females) were obtained from the 500-subject release of the Human Connectome Project (HCP RRID:SCR_008749) database from March 2015.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample size, demographics, and data source.

claim: Three stable subdivisions were identified in the SN of each hemisphere: a dorsolateral area corresponding to lateral part of SN pars compacta (lateral SNc), a dorsomedial area corresponding to medial part of SN pars compacta (medial SNc) and a ventral area (vSN).
source: Three stable subdivisions were identified in the SN of each hemisphere (Figure 2B): a dorsolateral area corresponding to lateral part of SN pars compacta (lateral SNc – hereafter: lSNc), a dorsomedial area corresponding to medial part of SN pars compacta (medial SNc - mSNc) and a ventral area (vSN).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectivity-based parcellation analysis shown in Figure 2B and described in the text.

claim: The tripartite separation of dorsomedial, lateral and ventral SN coincides with descriptions of dorsal, middle and ventral tiers of midbrain dopamine cells in primates.
source: This separation of dorsomedial, lateral and ventral SN coincides with descriptions of dorsal, middle and ventral tiers of midbrain dopamine cells in primates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which have distinct afferent and efferent striatal and cortical projections (Haber, 2014; Haber and Knutson, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published literature on primate anatomy.

claim: The three-subdivision parcellation of SN showed high reproducibility (mean normalized mutual information (NMI) = 0.85 and 0.88, respectively, for left and right SN).
source: As shown in Figure 2D, the three-subdivision parcellation of SN showed both high reproducibility (mean normalized mutual information (NMI) = 0.85 and 0.88, respectively, for left and right SN) and high inter-hemispheric topological similarity (mean NMI = 0.68).
evidence: Reproducibility was assessed using split-half resampling and quantified with NMI values.

claim: The three-subdivision parcellation of SN showed high inter-hemispheric topological similarity (mean NMI = 0.68).
source: As shown in Figure 2D, the three-subdivision parcellation of SN showed both high reproducibility (mean normalized mutual information (NMI) = 0.85 and 0.88, respectively, for left and right SN) and high inter-hemispheric topological similarity (mean NMI = 0.68).
evidence: Inter-hemispheric similarity was quantified using NMI.

claim: The replication of the parcellation procedure on a second group of 60 randomly selected subjects from the HCP dataset yielded very similar results (NMI = 0.95).
source: Finally, the replication of the parcellation procedure on a second group of 60 randomly selected subjects from the HCP dataset yielded very similar results (NMI = 0.95; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Replication analysis was performed on an independent sample.

claim: The dorsolateral subregion (lateral SNc) mainly connected with the somatic motor and sensory cortex in pre-/post-central gyrus.
source: Specifically, the dorsolateral subregion (i.e. lateral SNc) mainly connected with the somatic motor and sensory cortex in pre-/post-central gryus; the dorsomedial subregion (i.e. medial SNc) showed dominant connections with limbic regions including lateral and medial OFC, hippocampus and amygdala.
evidence: Connectivity patterns were determined using probabilistic fiber tractography.

claim: The dorsomedial subregion (medial SNc) showed dominant connections with limbic regions including lateral and medial OFC, hippocampus and amygdala.
source: Specifically, the dorsolateral subregion (i.e. lateral SNc) mainly connected with the somatic motor and sensory cortex in pre-/post-central gryus; the dorsomedial subregion (i.e. medial SNc) showed dominant connections with limbic regions including lateral and medial OFC, hippocampus and amygdala.
evidence: Connectivity patterns were determined using probabilistic fiber tractography.

claim: The ventral subregion (vSN) preferentially connected with prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex and anterior insula.
source: The ventral subregion (i.e. vSN) preferentially connected with prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex and anterior insula.
evidence: Connectivity patterns were determined using probabilistic fiber tractography.

claim: The connectivity maps reveal a limbic-cognitive-motor organizational topography of SN fiber projections.
source: These connectivity maps reveal a limbic-cognitive-motor organizational topography of SN fiber projections.
evidence: The organizational pattern is inferred from the connectivity data.

claim: The connectivity maps demonstrate a rotation in topology from medio-lateral in SN to ventro-dorsal (and rostro-caudal) in cortex.
source: They also demonstrate a rotation in topology from medio-lateral in SN to ventro-dorsal (and rostro-caudal) in cortex.
evidence: The topological pattern is observed in the connectivity data.

claim: In prefrontal cortex, a clear rosto-caudal pattern of SN projections was present, with medial SNc mainly connecting with the most rostral and ventral part including OFC and frontal pole.
source: Particularly, in prefrontal cortex, a clear rosto-caudal pattern of SN projections was present, with medial SNc mainly connecting with the most rostral and ventral part including OFC and frontal pole, vSN connecting to lateral and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex including middle frontal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus, and lateral SNc showing connections with the sensorimotor and somatosensory cortex.
evidence: The pattern is observed in the maximum probability map of tractograms.

claim: vSN connects to lateral and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex including middle frontal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus.
source: Particularly, in prefrontal cortex, a clear rosto-caudal pattern of SN projections was present, with medial SNc mainly connecting with the most rostral and ventral part including OFC and frontal pole, vSN connecting to lateral and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex including middle frontal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus, and lateral SNc showing connections with the sensorimotor and somatosensory cortex.
evidence: The pattern is observed in the maximum probability map of tractograms.

claim: Lateral SNc shows connections with the sensorimotor and somatosensory cortex.
source: Particularly, in prefrontal cortex, a clear rosto-caudal pattern of SN projections was present, with medial SNc mainly connecting with the most rostral and ventral part including OFC and frontal pole, vSN connecting to lateral and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex including middle frontal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus, and lateral SNc showing connections with the sensorimotor and somatosensory cortex.
evidence: The pattern is observed in the maximum probability map of tractograms.

claim: A similar rostro-caudal distribution of fiber tracts was seen in striatum, with medial SNc mainly connecting with ventral striatum.
source: A similar rostro-caudal distribution of fiber tracts was also seen in striatum, with medial SNc mainly connecting with ventral striatum, vSN connecting via the anterior limb of the internal capsule with the body of caudate and anterior part of putamen (associative striatum), and lateral SNc connecting via the posterior limb of the internal capsule with the posterior part of putamen (motor striatum).
evidence: The pattern is observed in the maximum probability map of tractograms.

claim: vSN connects via the anterior limb of the internal capsule with the body of caudate and anterior part of putamen (associative striatum).
source: A similar rostro-caudal distribution of fiber tracts was also seen in striatum, with medial SNc mainly connecting with ventral striatum, vSN connecting via the anterior limb of the internal capsule with the body of caudate and anterior part of putamen (associative striatum), and lateral SNc connecting via the posterior limb of the internal capsule with the posterior part of putamen (motor striatum).
evidence: The pattern is observed in the maximum probability map of tractograms.

claim: Lateral SNc connects via the posterior limb of the internal capsule with the posterior part of putamen (motor striatum).
source: A similar rostro-caudal distribution of fiber tracts was also seen in striatum, with medial SNc mainly connecting with ventral striatum, vSN connecting via the anterior limb of the internal capsule with the body of caudate and anterior part of putamen (associative striatum), and lateral SNc connecting via the posterior limb of the internal capsule with the posterior part of putamen (motor striatum).
evidence: The pattern is observed in the maximum probability map of tractograms.

claim: Medial SNc preferentially connected with the limbic and visual networks.
source: Specifically, medial SNc preferentially connected with the limbic and visual networks; vSN dominantly connected with the frontoparietal and default-mode networks; and lateral SNc mainly connected with the somatomotor and dorsal attention networks.
evidence: Connectivity to seven canonical resting-state networks was analyzed.

claim: vSN dominantly connected with the frontoparietal and default-mode networks.
source: Specifically, medial SNc preferentially connected with the limbic and visual networks; vSN dominantly connected with the frontoparietal and default-mode networks; and lateral SNc mainly connected with the somatomotor and dorsal attention networks.
evidence: Connectivity to seven canonical resting-state networks was analyzed.

claim: Lateral SNc mainly connected with the somatomotor and dorsal attention networks.
source: Specifically, medial SNc preferentially connected with the limbic and visual networks; vSN dominantly connected with the frontoparietal and default-mode networks; and lateral SNc mainly connected with the somatomotor and dorsal attention networks.
evidence: Connectivity to seven canonical resting-state networks was analyzed.

claim: All three SN subregions were activated by both reward and punishment.
source: As shown in Figure 6, all three SN subregions were activated by both reward and punishment, but only medial SNc showed significantly greater neural activity to monetary gains than losses (T = 3.96, p<0.0001).
evidence: BOLD responses during the gambling task were measured.

claim: Only medial SNc showed significantly greater neural activity to monetary gains than losses (T = 3.96, p<0.0001).
source: As shown in Figure 6, all three SN subregions were activated by both reward and punishment, but only medial SNc showed significantly greater neural activity to monetary gains than losses (T = 3.96, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of BOLD responses during the gambling task.

claim: Among the subdivisions of SN, medial SNc showed significantly higher BOLD response to positive value (gains) compared to the other two subdivisions (T = 3.52, p=0.0005 for vSN; T = 2.98, p=0.003 for lateral SNc).
source: Moreover, among the subdivisions of SN, medial SNc showed significantly higher BOLD response to positive value (gains) compared to the other two subdivisions (T = 3.52, p=0.0005 for vSN; T = 2.98, p=0.003 for lateral SNc), as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.
evidence: Statistical comparison of BOLD responses across SN subdivisions.

claim: Ventral striatum showed a unique bi-directional pattern, strongly activated during reward (T = 8.91, p<0.0001) and deactivated during punishment (T = −9.33, p<0.0001).
source: Specifically, ventral striatum showed a unique bi-directional pattern, i.e. strongly activated during reward (T = 8.91, p<0.0001) and deactivated during punishment (T = −9.33, p<0.0001).
evidence: BOLD responses in ventral striatum during the gambling task.

claim: vmPFC was deactivated in both reward and punishment conditions (T = −26.72 and −32.37 with p<0.0001 for reward and punishment, respectively).
source: Meanwhile, as a core region in the default mode network (DMN; [Buckner et al., 2008; Raichle, 2015]), vmPFC was deactivated in both conditions (T = −26.72 and −32.37 with p<0.0001 for reward and punishment, respectively).
evidence: BOLD responses in vmPFC during the gambling task.

claim: Both ventral striatum and vmPFC showed significantly greater response to rewarding than aversive outcomes (T = 16.25, p<0.0001 for ventral striatum, T = 8.75, p<0.00001 for vmPFC).
source: Both ventral striatum and vmPFC showed significantly greater response to rewarding than aversive outcomes (T = 16.25, p<0.0001 for ventral striatum, T = 8.75, p<0.00001 for vmPFC), although in the case of vmPFC this consisted of less deactivation (Figure 6).
evidence: Statistical comparison of BOLD responses to reward vs punishment.

claim: Of all regions examined, only VS showed the classic reward prediction error pattern (activation for gains, inhibition for losses).
source: Of all regions examined, only VS showed the classic reward prediction error pattern (activation for gains, inhibition for losses).
evidence: Analysis of BOLD response patterns across regions.

claim: dACC and anterior insula were activated by both types of trials, with no difference in response to reward and punishment (T = 1.37, p=0.17 for dACC, T = 1.07, p=0.28 for anterior insula).
source: On the contrary, as the core areas of the salience network (Seeley et al., 2007), dACC and anterior insula were activated by both types of trials, with no difference in response to reward and punishment (T = 1.37, p=0.17 for dACC, T = 1.07, p=0.28 for anterior insula).
evidence: Statistical analysis of BOLD responses in salience network regions.

claim: There are at least two separate brain dopamine-related systems involved during gambling outcomes, with one encoding reward value and the other encoding motivational salience.
source: These results support the theory that there are at least two separate brain dopamine-related systems involved during gambling outcomes, with one encoding reward value (i.e. different response to reward and punishment) and the other encoding motivational salience (i.e. reacting similarly to rewarding and aversive outcomes).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of BOLD responses across regions.

claim: Two components were identified by behavioral PLS analysis (proportion of covariance = 61% and 39%, permuted p-value=0.012 and 0.11, respectively).
source: Two components were identified (Figure 7, proportion of covariance = 61% and 39%, permuted p-value=0.012 and 0.11, respectively), with one significantly correlated with inhibitory control scores (r = 0.1896, CI= [0.1575, 0.2781]) while the other was significantly correlated with Delay-Discounting measures (r = −0.1535, CI= [−0.2499,–0.1277]).
evidence: Behavioral PLS analysis was performed on BOLD activity and impulsivity measures.

claim: One component was significantly correlated with inhibitory control scores (r = 0.1896, CI= [0.1575, 0.2781]).
source: Two components were identified (Figure 7, proportion of covariance = 61% and 39%, permuted p-value=0.012 and 0.11, respectively), with one significantly correlated with inhibitory control scores (r = 0.1896, CI= [0.1575, 0.2781]) while the other was significantly correlated with Delay-Discounting measures (r = −0.1535, CI= [−0.2499,–0.1277]).
evidence: Behavioral PLS analysis results.

claim: One component was significantly correlated with Delay-Discounting measures (r = −0.1535, CI= [−0.2499,–0.1277]).
source: Two components were identified (Figure 7, proportion of covariance = 61% and 39%, permuted p-value=0.012 and 0.11, respectively), with one significantly correlated with inhibitory control scores (r = 0.1896, CI= [0.1575, 0.2781]) while the other was significantly correlated with Delay-Discounting measures (r = −0.1535, CI= [−0.2499,–0.1277]).
evidence: Behavioral PLS analysis results.

claim: The first component (inhibitory control) comprised the value signal from vmPFC (z-score of weights = 2.1482) and salience signal from insula (z-score = 2.5006) and dACC (z = 2.7626).
source: The first component (inhibitory control) comprised the value signal from vmPFC (z-score of weights = 2.1482) and salience signal from insula (z-score = 2.5006) and dACC (z = 2.7626).
evidence: Behavioral PLS analysis identified brain regions contributing to each component.

claim: The second component (delay-discounting) comprised the value signal from mSNc (z-score = 2.0518) and VS (z-score = 2.5937).
source: The second component (delay-discounting) comprised the value signal from mSNc (z-score = 2.0518) and VS (z-score = 2.5937).
evidence: Behavioral PLS analysis identified brain regions contributing to each component.

claim: Significant correlations were found between AUC of Delay Discounting and value-related BOLD response in medial SNc (r = −0.1304, p=0.0053) and ventral striatum (r = −0.1191, p=0.01).
source: We found significant correlations between AUC of Delay Discounting and value-related BOLD response in medial SNc (r = −0.1304, p=0.0053) and ventral striatum (r = −0.1191, p=0.01), and correlations between inhibitory control scores and salience-related BOLD response in dACC (r = 0.1112, p=0.0161) and anterior insula (r = 0.1546, p=0.0008).
evidence: Individual correlation analyses between BOLD responses and impulsivity measures.

claim: Correlations were found between inhibitory control scores and salience-related BOLD response in dACC (r = 0.1112, p=0.0161) and anterior insula (r = 0.1546, p=0.0008).
source: We found significant correlations between AUC of Delay Discounting and value-related BOLD response in medial SNc (r = −0.1304, p=0.0053) and ventral striatum (r = −0.1191, p=0.01), and correlations between inhibitory control scores and salience-related BOLD response in dACC (r = 0.1112, p=0.0161) and anterior insula (r = 0.1546, p=0.0008).
evidence: Individual correlation analyses between BOLD responses and impulsivity measures.

claim: Only the associations of value-coding response in mSNc with Delay-Discounting and salience-coding response in insula with inhibitory control remain significant after Holm–Bonferroni correction with p-value=0.05.
source: Only the associations of value-coding response in mSNc with Delay-Discounting and salience-coding response in insula with inhibitory control remain significant after Holm–Bonferroni correction with p-value=0.05.
evidence: Multiple comparison correction was applied to correlation results.

claim: The correlation of value-coding response in VS was significantly higher with Delay-Discounting measures than inhibitory control scores (p=0.02).
source: Moreover, the correlation of value-coding response in VS was significantly higher with Delay-Discounting measures than inhibitory control scores (p=0.02), while the association of salience-coding response in anterior insula was significantly stronger with inhibitory control than Delay-Discounting (p=0.008).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlations between different behavioral measures.

claim: The association of salience-coding response in anterior insula was significantly stronger with inhibitory control than Delay-Discounting (p=0.008).
source: Moreover, the correlation of value-coding response in VS was significantly higher with Delay-Discounting measures than inhibitory control scores (p=0.02), while the association of salience-coding response in anterior insula was significantly stronger with inhibitory control than Delay-Discounting (p=0.008).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlations between different behavioral measures.

claim: In monkeys, SN neurons can be divided into three tiers based on their staining, morphology, and connectivity with the striatum.
source: In monkeys, SN/VTA dopamine neurons display variations in both anatomy and function. SN neurons can be divided into three tiers based on their staining, morphology, and connectivity with the striatum (Haber, 2014; Haber and Knutson, 2010): moving from a dorso-medial to ventro-lateral location in midbrain, dopamine neurons project to limbic, associative and then motor striatum.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on monkey anatomy.

claim: Moving from a dorso-medial to ventro-lateral location in midbrain, dopamine neurons project to limbic, associative and then motor striatum.
source: In monkeys, SN/VTA dopamine neurons display variations in both anatomy and function. SN neurons can be divided into three tiers based on their staining, morphology, and connectivity with the striatum (Haber, 2014; Haber and Knutson, 2010): moving from a dorso-medial to ventro-lateral location in midbrain, dopamine neurons project to limbic, associative and then motor striatum.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on monkey anatomy.

claim: All three subdivisions send dendrites ventrally into the adjacent SN pars reticulata.
source: All three subdivisions send dendrites ventrally into the adjacent SN pars reticulata (Haber and Knutson, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cells in ventromedial SNc and VTA encode a value signal, being excited by appetitive events and inhibited by aversive events.
source: Distinct functional characteristics have also been reported for SN/VTA neurons by recording neural activity during appetitive and aversive outcomes (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Nomoto et al., 2010). Cells in ventromedial SNc and VTA encode a value signal, being excited by appetitive events and inhibited by aversive events.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to electrophysiology studies in monkeys.

claim: Neurons in lateral SN may encode a salience signal, responding equally to appetitive and aversive stimuli.
source: Neurons in lateral SN may encode a salience signal, responding equally to appetitive and aversive stimuli.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature context provided earlier in the paragraph.

claim: Dopamine plays a crucial role in decision-making and reinforcement learning by encoding a reward-prediction error signal.
source: Dopamine plays a crucial role in decision-making and reinforcement learning by encoding a reward-prediction error signal (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Glimcher, 2011; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The role of dopamine in motivational and cognitive processing has been extended by descriptions of responses not only to rewarding outcomes but also to novel, salient, and possibly aversive experiences.
source: More recently, the role of dopamine in motivational and cognitive processing has been extended by descriptions of responses not only to rewarding outcomes but also to novel, salient, and possibly aversive experiences (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Lisman and Grace, 2005; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Redgrave and Gurney, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Impulsivity is defined as a tendency to act rapidly and prematurely without appropriate foresight.
source: An important clinical aspect of dopamine signaling is its role in impulsivity, defined as a tendency to act rapidly and prematurely without appropriate foresight (Dagher and Robbins, 2009; Dalley and Robbins, 2017; Morris and Voon, 2016).
evidence: The definition is provided with supporting citations.

claim: Impulsivity is a key feature of drug addiction, obesity, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
source: Impulsivity is a key feature of drug addiction, obesity, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Impulsivity can be divided into different components.
source: It can be divided into different components (Meda et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Decisional impulsivity is characterized by a tendency to make maladaptive or inappropriate choices and is typically tested with the Delay Discounting task.
source: Decisional impulsivity is characterized by a tendency to make maladaptive or inappropriate choices and is typically tested with the Delay Discounting task.
evidence: The definition and measurement method are provided.

claim: Motor impulsivity refers to premature responding or an inability to inhibit an inappropriate action, and can be tested using Go/No Go type tasks.
source: Motor impulsivity, on the other hand, refers to premature responding or an inability to inhibit an inappropriate action, and can be tested using Go/No Go type tasks.
evidence: The definition and measurement method are provided.

claim: VS and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), which encode stimulus value, are implicated in decisional impulsivity.
source: Discrete neural networks may underlie different forms of impulsivity: VS and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), which encode stimulus value, are implicated in decisional impulsivity (Kable and Glimcher, 2007; McClure et al., 2004; Sellitto et al., 2010); somatomotor cortex, supplementary motor area (SMA), inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), anterior insula and dorsal striatum are thought to play a role in motor impulsivity (Bari and Robbins, 2013; Cai et al., 2014; Chikazoe et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Somatomotor cortex, supplementary motor area (SMA), inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), anterior insula and dorsal striatum are thought to play a role in motor impulsivity.
source: Discrete neural networks may underlie different forms of impulsivity: VS and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), which encode stimulus value, are implicated in decisional impulsivity (Kable and Glimcher, 2007; McClure et al., 2004; Sellitto et al., 2010); somatomotor cortex, supplementary motor area (SMA), inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), anterior insula and dorsal striatum are thought to play a role in motor impulsivity (Bari and Robbins, 2013; Cai et al., 2014; Chikazoe et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: All brain regions implicated in impulsivity are interconnected with SN: they receive dopamine innervation and send back direct or indirect projections that can modulate dopamine neuron activity.
source: All these brain regions are interconnected with SN: they receive dopamine innervation and send back direct or indirect projections that can modulate dopamine neuron activity (Haber and Knutson, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A similar anatomical and connectional differentiation of SN has been widely described in monkeys.
source: A similar anatomical and connectional differentiation of SN has been widely described in monkeys.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from primate studies.

claim: Many studies report that midbrain dopamine neurons can be divided into two or three tiers.
source: Indeed, many studies report that midbrain dopamine neurons can be divided into two or three tiers (François et al., 1999; Haber and Knutson, 2010; Lynd-Balta and Haber, 1994), with a dorsal calbindin-positive tier that extends medially to the VTA, and a ventral calbindin-negative tier whose dendrites extend ventrally into the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Midbrain dopamine neurons include a dorsal calbindin-positive tier that extends medially to the VTA, and a ventral calbindin-negative tier whose dendrites extend ventrally into the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra.
source: Indeed, many studies report that midbrain dopamine neurons can be divided into two or three tiers (François et al., 1999; Haber and Knutson, 2010; Lynd-Balta and Haber, 1994), with a dorsal calbindin-positive tier that extends medially to the VTA, and a ventral calbindin-negative tier whose dendrites extend ventrally into the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ventral tier can be further subdivided into a more medio-dorsal densocellular group and a ventro-lateral group of columnar cells.
source: This ventral tier can be further subdivided into a more medio-dorsal densocellular group and a ventro-lateral group of columnar cells (Haber, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Tracer studies in monkeys have been used to map the striatal afferent and efferent projections of SN subdivisions.
source: Tracer studies in monkeys have been used to map the striatal afferent and efferent projections of these SN subdivisions (Haber et al., 2000; Haber and Knutson, 2010; Lynd-Balta and Haber, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In monkeys, the dorsal tier mainly connects with ventromedial striatum, while the ventral tiers project to central and dorsolateral striatum.
source: The dorsal tier mainly connects with ventromedial striatum, while the ventral tiers project to central and dorsolateral striatum.
evidence: The claim is based on tracer studies in monkeys cited in the previous sentence.

claim: The mSNc corresponds to the monkey pars dorsalis and connects with ventral striatum.
source: Specifically, our mSNc corresponds to the monkey pars dorsalis and connects with ventral striatum; lSNc corresponds to the ventrolateral columnar part of SNc and connects to the motor regions of dorsal striatum.
evidence: The correspondence is inferred from comparing human and monkey anatomy.

claim: lSNc corresponds to the ventrolateral columnar part of SNc and connects to the motor regions of dorsal striatum.
source: Specifically, our mSNc corresponds to the monkey pars dorsalis and connects with ventral striatum; lSNc corresponds to the ventrolateral columnar part of SNc and connects to the motor regions of dorsal striatum.
evidence: The correspondence is inferred from comparing human and monkey anatomy.

claim: vSN corresponds to the ventral densocellular portion that projects to the middle, associative, part of the striatum.
source: Finally, our vSN corresponds to the ventral densocellular portion that projects to the middle, associative, part of the striatum (Haber, 2014).
evidence: The correspondence is inferred from comparing human and monkey anatomy.

claim: The specific association of lSNc with sensorimotor cortex explains its crucial role in the motor symptoms of Parkinson disease, in which ventrolateral SNc is preferentially targeted by neurodegeneration.
source: This specific association of lSNc with sensorimotor cortex explains its crucial role in the motor symptoms of Parkinson disease, in which ventrolateral SNc is preferentially targeted by neurodegeneration (Gibb and Lees, 1991).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the connectivity findings and supported by citation to Parkinson's disease literature.

claim: vmPFC is a connectional hub that integrates broad domains of information to support the valuation process during decision-making.
source: This is consistent with the view that vmPFC is a connectional hub that integrates broad domains of information to support the valuation process during decision-making (Benoit et al., 2014; Roy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The inverted dorsal/ventral topography of SN-striatum connections has previously been described in human brain.
source: The inverted dorsal/ventral topography of SN-striatum connections (Haber, 2014) found here has previously been described in human brain (Chowdhury et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In a previous human study, the dorsal SN mainly connected to ventral striatum, while the ventral SN preferentially connected to dorsal striatum.
source: There, the authors used diffusion tractography in 30 individuals to parcellate SN based on anatomical connections with two targets in striatum. The dorsal SN mainly connected to ventral striatum, while the ventral SN preferentially connected to dorsal striatum.
evidence: The claim describes findings from a cited study.

claim: Two distinct fiber tracts were found projecting through SN: the frontopontine tract (FPT) connecting prefrontal cortex and anterior SN and running through the anterior limb of the internal capsule, and the corticospinal tract (CST) connecting motor cortex and posterior SN and passing through the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
source: Recently, whole-brain tractography was also performed on the HCP dataset to identify the major brainstem white matter tracts (Meola et al., 2016). Two distinct fiber tracts were found projecting through SN: the frontopontine tract (FPT) connecting prefrontal cortex and anterior SN and running through the anterior limb of the internal capsule, and the corticospinal tract (CST) connecting motor cortex and posterior SN and passing through the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
evidence: The claim describes findings from a cited study.

claim: The midbrain projections to visual cortex are sparse in rodents.
source: For instance, the midbrain projections to visual cortex are sparse in rodents (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012), but we detected relatively strong anatomical connections between mSNc and visual areas using both probabilistic and deterministic tractography (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to rodent literature.

claim: Relatively strong anatomical connections were detected between mSNc and visual areas using both probabilistic and deterministic tractography.
source: For instance, the midbrain projections to visual cortex are sparse in rodents (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012), but we detected relatively strong anatomical connections between mSNc and visual areas using both probabilistic and deterministic tractography (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is based on tractography results.

claim: The detected connections between mSNc and visual areas might be caused by an intersection of mSNc outflow with the temporo-parieto-occipito-pontine tract in the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
source: This might be caused by an intersection of mSNc outflow with the temporo-parieto-occipito-pontine tract in the posterior limb of the internal capsule (Meola et al., 2016).
evidence: The explanation is speculative, based on known anatomy.
